dropped.reason: Wave terminology: crest to trough (Year 11 Module 3).

questions.question: The centripetal force that causes a car to go round a bend in the road is provided by
questions.answer: On a flat bend the net force towards the centre of the curve is the sideways (static) friction between the tyres and the road (B). The engine force acts along the direction of motion, and the weight acts vertically.
options: the force produced by the car engine acting on the wheels.
the friction between the tyres and the road.
the force exerted by the driver on the steering wheel.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a true statement concerning the vertical component of the velocity and the acceleration of a projectile when it is at its maximum height? (The acceleration of free fall is $g$.)
questions.answer: At the top of its flight the vertical velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is $g$ downwards (D).

questions.question: Electric field strength is defined as
questions.answer: $\mathbf E=\dfrac{\mathbf F}q$ is the force per unit charge acting on a positive test charge, which also fixes the direction of the field (D).
options: the force exerted on a test charge.
the force per unit positive charge.
the force per unit charge exerted on a positive test charge.

questions.question: Two positive point charges P and Q are held a certain distance apart, in the order X, P, Y, Q, Z along a line (Y lies between P and Q; X is beyond P and Z beyond Q). At which point(s) could the electric field strength, due to the charges, be zero?
questions.answer: Outside the two charges (X and Z) both fields point away from the charges in the same direction, so they add and cannot cancel. Between the charges (Y) the fields point in opposite directions and can cancel at the right position (B).

questions.question: High voltages are used for the transmission of electric power over long distances because
questions.answer: For a given power $P=VI$, a higher voltage means a smaller current, and the power loss in the lines is $I^2R$, so losses are minimised (C).
options: high voltages can be stepped down to any required value.
power losses during transmission are minimized.

questions.question: A thin copper ring encloses an area $S$. The area is linked by magnetic flux that is increasing. The rate of change of the magnetic flux from time $t=0$ to time $t=T$ is $R$. The emf induced in the copper ring during the time $t=0$ to time $t=T$ is
questions.answer: Faraday's law: $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. The rate of change of flux is given as $R$, and $N=1$, so the magnitude of the emf is $R$ (A).

questions.question: The unit, the electron-volt is equivalent to
questions.answer: One electron-volt is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V: $W=qV=1.6\times10^{-19}\times1=1.6\times10^{-19}$ J (C).

questions.question: The diagram shows the path of a projectile in the absence of air resistance. Which one of the following diagrams best represents the path of the projectile under the same initial conditions when the air resistance is taken into account? (The path in absence of air resistance is shown dotted.)
questions.answer: Air resistance reduces both the horizontal and the vertical velocity components. The projectile reaches a lower maximum height and a shorter range, and the path is asymmetric: it falls more steeply than it rises. Path A shows this (B is wrong since it has the same maximum height; C and D have a longer or equal range) (A).

questions.question: A person is walking along one side of a building and a car is driving along another side of the building. The person can hear the car approach but cannot see it. This is explained by the fact that light waves
questions.answer: Diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the gap or obstacle. Sound waves have wavelengths of the order of metres, so they bend (diffract) around the corner of a building, while light has a wavelength of about $10^{-7}$ m and hardly diffracts at all (B).
options: travel much faster than sound waves.
are diffracted less at the corner of the building than sound waves.
are refracted less at the corner of the building than sound waves.

questions.question: A charged particle P is accelerated between two charged metal plates X and Y separated by a distance $d$. The particle starts from rest at plate X. The kinetic energy of P, when it reaches plate Y, is $K$. The magnitude of the charge on P is $e$. The magnitude of the electric field strength between the plates is
questions.answer: Work done by the field $=Fd=eEd=K$, so $E=\dfrac K{ed}$ (C).

questions.question: The work function of a metal may be defined as
questions.answer: The work function $\phi$ is the minimum photon energy that can cause photoelectric emission, $\phi=hf_0$, where $f_0$ is the threshold frequency (C). A describes the threshold frequency, and B is not a meaningful definition (it would be a maximum wavelength).
options: the minimum frequency of the incident electromagnetic radiation required to cause photoelectric emission.
the minimum wavelength of the incident electromagnetic radiation required to cause photoelectric emission.
the minimum energy of photons incident on a surface required to cause photoelectric emission.
the minimum energy required to take an electron from the interior to the surface to cause photoelectric emission.

questions.question: Which of the following graphs best shows how photon energy $E$ varies with the wavelength $\lambda$ of the light?
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac{hc}\lambda$, so $E$ is inversely proportional to $\lambda$: a decreasing curve (hyperbola) that approaches both axes without touching them (D).

questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ is incident on a polariser. The transmitted light is then incident on a second polariser. The axis of the second polariser makes an angle of $60^\circ$ to the axis of the first polariser. The cosine of $60^\circ$ is $\tfrac12$. The intensity of the light transmitted through the second polariser is
questions.answer: The first polariser transmits half of the unpolarised light: $\dfrac{I_0}2$. Malus' law for the second: $I=I_{max}\cos^2\theta=\dfrac{I_0}2\times\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=\dfrac{I_0}8$ (D).

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC electric motor. The armature is a single rectangular coil that rotates between the poles of a permanent magnet. The split-ring commutator is labelled C, and the connections between the coil and the battery B are not shown. Describe how the battery B must be connected to the split-ring so that the coil will rotate continuously in one direction.
questions.answer: The two terminals of the battery are connected to the two halves of the split ring through brushes (conducting spring-loaded contacts) which press on the split ring on opposite sides.

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC electric motor with the armature in the position shown (the coil is horizontal between the N and S poles). When the connection to the battery is made, state the directions of the forces acting on the two sides of the coil that lie in the magnetic field (the sides parallel to the axle).
questions.answer: The currents in the two sides are in opposite directions, so by the motor effect the forces on them are in opposite directions: one side is pushed up and the other is pushed down. These forces form a couple (torque) that rotates the coil about its axle (the school's diagram shows an upward arrow on the right-hand side and a downward arrow on the left-hand side).

questions.question: In a simple DC motor, the battery is connected to the split-ring commutator through brushes. Describe how these connections enable the coil to rotate continuously in one direction.
questions.answer: While each half of the split ring is in contact with a brush, the current in the coil flows in one direction and the torque turns the coil. After the coil has rotated through $180^\circ$ the sides of the coil have swapped places, and the commutator has swapped which side is connected to which brush, so the current in the coil reverses (the current in the side nearest the north pole is always in the same direction). The torque therefore always acts in the same rotational sense. When the gaps in the split ring are passing the brushes, no current flows and the momentum of the coil carries it through the position of zero torque.

questions.question: In an experiment to measure the efficiency of a small DC electric motor, the motor is used to raise a small weight attached to a pulley wheel by cotton thread. The running current in the motor is adjusted to 0.3 A so that a weight of mass 150 g is raised at constant speed. The motor is connected to a 6.0 V supply and the weight is raised through 0.84 m. If the motor's armature windings have a total resistance of 5.0 $\Omega$, calculate the start-up current. Calculate the back emf induced in the motor during lifting.
questions.answer: At start-up the coil is not yet rotating, so there is no back emf: $I=\dfrac VR=\dfrac{6.0}{5.0}=1.2$ A. While running, $V_{supply}=\varepsilon_{back}+IR$, so $\varepsilon_{back}=6.0-0.3\times5.0=4.5$ V.

questions.question: In an experiment to measure the efficiency of a small DC electric motor, the motor is used to raise a small weight attached to a pulley wheel by cotton thread. The running current in the motor is adjusted to 0.3 A so that a weight of mass 150 g is raised at constant speed. The motor is connected to a 6.0 V supply and the weight is raised through 0.84 m. If it takes the motor 3.4 s to raise the weight, determine the power delivered to the weight by the motor.
questions.answer: Gain in gravitational potential energy $=mgh=0.150\times9.8\times0.84=1.23$ J. $P=\dfrac Et=\dfrac{1.23}{3.4}=0.36$ W.

questions.question: In an experiment to measure the efficiency of a small DC electric motor, the motor is used to raise a small weight attached to a pulley wheel by cotton thread. The running current in the motor is adjusted to 0.3 A so that a weight of mass 150 g is raised at constant speed. The motor is connected to a 6.0 V supply and the weight is raised through 0.84 m. Estimate the efficiency of the motor.
questions.answer: Input power $=VI=6.0\times0.3=1.8$ W. Efficiency $=\dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}=\dfrac{0.36}{1.8}=0.20$, i.e. 20%.

questions.question: State one aspect of the photoelectric effect that cannot be explained by the wave model of light. Describe how the photon model provides an explanation for this aspect.
questions.answer: Aspect (any one): electrons are not emitted unless the frequency of the light exceeds a certain minimum (threshold) value; or electrons are emitted almost instantaneously, even for light of very low intensity; or the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons is not affected by the intensity of the light. Explanation (matching the aspect): light consists of photons of energy $hf$, and each electron absorbs a single photon. No electrons are emitted unless $hf$ is larger than the energy needed to escape the metal (the work function); an electron is emitted as soon as it absorbs a photon of sufficient energy, so there is no delay; and the kinetic energy of an emitted electron depends only on the photon energy (the frequency), while the intensity only changes the number of photons and so the number of electrons.

questions.question: Light is incident on a metal surface in a vacuum. The graph shows the variation of the maximum kinetic energy $E_{max}$ of the electrons emitted from the surface with the frequency $f$ of the incident light. The line passes through about (6, 0.9) and (13.6, 4.0) (frequency in units of $10^{14}$ Hz, energy in eV). Use data from the graph to determine the threshold frequency.
questions.answer: The threshold frequency is the frequency-axis intercept of the line (extended back to $E_{max}=0$): $f_0=3.8\ (\pm0.2)\times10^{14}$ Hz.

questions.question: Light is incident on a metal surface in a vacuum. The graph shows the variation of the maximum kinetic energy $E_{max}$ of the electrons emitted from the surface with the frequency $f$ of the incident light. The line passes through about (6, 0.9) and (13.6, 4.0) (frequency in units of $10^{14}$ Hz, energy in eV). Use data from the graph to determine a value of the Planck constant.
questions.answer: From $E_{max}=hf-\phi$, $h$ is the gradient of the graph: $\dfrac{(4.0-0.9)\ \text{eV}}{(13.6-6.0)\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}}=4.1\times10^{-15}$ eV s $=4.1\times10^{-15}\times1.6\times10^{-19}=6.5\ (\pm0.2)\times10^{-34}$ J s.

questions.question: Light is incident on a metal surface in a vacuum. The graph shows the variation of the maximum kinetic energy $E_{max}$ of the electrons emitted from the surface with the frequency $f$ of the incident light. The line passes through about (6, 0.9) and (13.6, 4.0) (frequency in units of $10^{14}$ Hz, energy in eV). Use data from the graph to determine the work function of the surface.
questions.answer: The work function is the magnitude of the vertical-axis intercept (extrapolating the line back to $f=0$): $\phi=1.5\ (\pm0.1)$ eV. (Check: $\phi=hf_0=4.1\times10^{-15}\times3.8\times10^{14}=1.6$ eV.)

questions.question: Light is incident on a metal surface in a vacuum. The graph shows the variation of the maximum kinetic energy $E_{max}$ of the electrons emitted from the surface with the frequency $f$ of the incident light. The line passes through about (6, 0.9) and (13.6, 4.0) (frequency in units of $10^{14}$ Hz, energy in eV). The threshold frequency of a different surface is $8.0\times10^{14}$ Hz. Describe the line showing the variation with frequency $f$ of the maximum kinetic energy $E_{max}$ of the electrons emitted from this surface (on the same axes).
questions.answer: A straight line parallel to the first (the gradient is still the Planck constant $h$), meeting the frequency axis at $8.0\times10^{14}$ Hz. It is the first line shifted to the right; extended back it would meet the vertical axis at $-hf_0=-3.3$ eV, and there is no emission below $8.0\times10^{14}$ Hz.

questions.question: Saturn has several rings, each of which consists of many small particles that orbit the planet. Saturn may be considered to be a sphere with its mass $M$ concentrated at its centre. Deduce that, for a particle in one ring moving in a circular orbit of radius $R$, the linear speed $v$ of the particle in its orbit is given by $GM=Rv^2$. Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: The gravitational force of Saturn on the particle provides the centripetal force that keeps it in a circular orbit: $\dfrac{mv^2}R=\dfrac{GMm}{R^2}$. Cancelling $m$ and one factor of $R$ gives $GM=Rv^2$.

questions.question: The A ring of Saturn has an outer diameter of $2.72\times10^8$ m. The mass of Saturn is $5.69\times10^{26}$ kg. A particle orbits on the outer edge of this ring. Determine the time for the particle to complete one orbit of Saturn.
questions.answer: $R=\dfrac{2.72\times10^8}2=1.36\times10^8$ m. $v^2=\dfrac{GM}R=\dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times5.69\times10^{26}}{1.36\times10^8}=2.79\times10^8$, so $v=1.67\times10^4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $T=\dfrac{2\pi R}v=\dfrac{2\pi\times1.36\times10^8}{1.67\times10^4}=5.1\times10^4$ s (about 14 hours).

questions.question: Explain the concept of escape speed.
questions.answer: Escape speed is the minimum speed that an object must be given at the surface of a planet in order to move to infinity, i.e. completely escape the planet's gravitational field (arriving there with zero speed), without further propulsion.

questions.question: A planet has radius $R$ and the acceleration of free fall at its surface is $g$. The planet may be considered to be a sphere with its mass concentrated at its centre. Deduce that the escape speed $v_{es}$ is given by $v_{es}=\sqrt{2gR}$. Explain your working and state one assumption that is made in the derivation.
questions.answer: To escape, the kinetic energy at the surface must equal the gain in gravitational potential energy in moving to infinity (where $U=0$): $\tfrac12mv^2=\dfrac{GMm}R$ (the loss of kinetic energy equals the gain in potential energy; $mgh$ is not appropriate here as $g$ is not constant). Then $v^2=\dfrac{2GM}R$. At the surface $g=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, so $GM=gR^2$ and $v_{es}=\sqrt{2gR}$. Assumption: the planet is isolated (no other bodies), has no atmosphere (no air resistance), and does not rotate or move.

questions.question: Calculate the escape speed for a spherical planet of radius $1.7\times10^3$ km having an acceleration of free fall at its surface of $1.6\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
questions.answer: $v_{es}=\sqrt{2gR}=\sqrt{2\times1.6\times1.7\times10^6}=2.3\times10^3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: State the two postulates of the special theory of relativity.
questions.answer: Postulate 1: all inertial frames of reference are equivalent (the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames). Postulate 2: the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant, the same for all observers regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

questions.question: A super-fast spacecraft is moving at a speed of $0.80c$ with respect to observers on Earth. The spacecraft leaves Earth in May 2004 on its way to a distant solar system. According to the observers in the spacecraft, 6.0 years have elapsed since leaving Earth. Calculate the time elapsed according to an observer on Earth.
questions.answer: The spacecraft observers measure the proper time $t_0=6.0$ years. $\gamma=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-0.8^2}}=\dfrac1{0.6}=\dfrac{10}6$. $t=\gamma t_0=\dfrac{10}6\times6.0=10$ years.

questions.question: A super-fast spacecraft is moving at a speed of $0.80c$ with respect to observers on Earth. The spacecraft leaves Earth in May 2004 on its way to a distant solar system. The time elapsed is 6.0 years according to the spacecraft observers and 10 years according to Earth observers. Explain whether either measured time interval can be considered to be 'correct'.
questions.answer: Both are correct. Both sets of observers are in inertial frames of reference, and by the first postulate there is no preferred frame. Each is a valid measurement in its own frame (the 6.0 years is the proper time, as measured by a single clock at the spacecraft).

questions.question: A super-fast spacecraft is moving at a speed of $0.80c$ with respect to observers on Earth. The spacecraft leaves Earth in May 2004 on its way to a distant solar system. Calculate the distance of the spacecraft from Earth according to an observer on Earth.
questions.answer: According to Earth observers the spacecraft has been travelling for 10 years at $0.80c$: $d=vt=0.80c\times10\ \text{y}=8.0$ light years $(=7.6\times10^{16}$ m$)$.

questions.question: A super-fast spacecraft is moving at a speed of $0.80c$ with respect to observers on Earth. The spacecraft leaves Earth in May 2004 on its way to a distant solar system. The observers in the spacecraft send a radio message to Earth to say that they have been travelling for 6.0 years. Determine how long it will take the message to get to Earth according to the spacecraft observers.
questions.answer: In the spacecraft frame, when the message is sent Earth is receding at $0.80c$ and is a distance $0.80c\times6.0=4.8$ light years away. The message travels at $c$: $cT=4.8c+0.80cT$, so $0.20T=4.8$ and $T=24$ years. (Check in the Earth frame: the message is sent when the spacecraft is 8.0 light years away, at Earth time 10 years, and reaches Earth 8 years later, at 18 years after departure. For the events 'departure' and 'message arrives' (both at Earth), 18 years is the proper time in the Earth frame, so the spacecraft clocks show $\gamma\times18=30$ years between them, which is 24 years after the 6 years at which the message was sent.)

questions.question: A small ball of mass 1.8 kg travels in a horizontal circular path at constant speed while attached to a vertical rod by a 0.75 m long string (at $25^\circ$ to the rod) on a frictionless sleeve. Describe (or indicate with labelled arrows) the two physical forces acting on the ball.
questions.answer: The tension in the string (along the string, up and towards the rod) and the weight $mg$ (vertically downwards). The centripetal force is not a separate physical force; it is the horizontal component of the tension.

questions.question: A small ball of mass 1.8 kg travels in a horizontal circular path at constant speed while attached to a vertical rod by a 0.75 m long string, which makes an angle of $25^\circ$ with the rod, on a frictionless sleeve. Derive a suitable expression and use it to calculate the speed of the ball.
questions.answer: Vertically: $T\cos\theta=mg$. Horizontally (towards the centre): $T\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}r$. Dividing, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{gr}$, i.e. $v^2=gr\tan\theta$. With $r=0.75\sin25^\circ=0.317$ m: $v^2=9.8\times0.317\times\tan25^\circ=1.45$, so $v=1.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: A second string of the same length (0.75 m) is now attached to the rod and the mass (see diagram), each string making $30^\circ$ with the rod and T$_1$ being the upper string and T$_2$ the lower string, using frictionless sleeves. The mass of 1.8 kg rotates in a horizontal circle with a constant speed of $3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the tension in each string, $T_1$ and $T_2$. Show your working.
questions.answer: The radius is $r=0.75\sin30^\circ=0.375$ m. Vertically (no vertical acceleration): the upper string pulls up and the lower string pulls down: $T_1\cos30^\circ=T_2\cos30^\circ+mg$, so $T_1-T_2=\dfrac{1.8\times9.8}{\cos30^\circ}=20.4$ N. Horizontally, both strings pull towards the rod: $(T_1+T_2)\sin30^\circ=\dfrac{mv^2}r=\dfrac{1.8\times3.0^2}{0.375}=43.2$ N, so $T_1+T_2=86.4$ N. Solving: $T_1=53.4$ N and $T_2=33.0$ N.

questions.question: The diagram shows a model of electromagnetic waves (an oscillating charge $q$ producing perpendicular, in-phase electric and magnetic field oscillations $E_0$ and $B_0$ propagating along $x$). Relate this model to predictions made by Maxwell.
questions.answer: Any four of: (i) The diagram shows electric and magnetic fields oscillating perpendicular to each other, relating to Maxwell's prediction that a changing electric field induces a changing magnetic field and vice versa, so that the wave is self-propagating. (ii) The electric and magnetic fields are in phase: at any point they both reach their maximum value at the same time. (iii) The wave propagates in a direction perpendicular to both the electric and magnetic fields, at the speed $c=\dfrac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$. (iv) Maxwell predicted a whole range of electromagnetic waves with different wavelengths, all travelling at the same speed $c$ in a vacuum. (v) The wave is produced by an oscillating (accelerating) charge, which produces changing electric and magnetic fields, consistent with Maxwell's prediction that oscillating charges produce electromagnetic radiation.
